items.summary:

Starting today, we're offering free Kimi API credits to support scientific research worldwide.

Selected teams will receive free Kimi API credits, access to our latest models, and opportunities for long-term collaboration.

The program builds on our commitment to open-weight models by making frontier AI more accessible to researchers.

AI has the potential to change what can be studied, who can study it, and at what scale, making it possible to pursue a wider range of scientific questions with limited resources.

Both theoretical and experimental research in fundamental science and engineering are welcome. We hope to help researchers take on more challenging and original questions, including those that have historically received less attention or funding.

Apply by Dec 8 for the first round: kimi.ai/news/kimi-for-scienc…

·

Open to researchers at all career stages, including PhD students, postdocs, and PIs. Credits will be provided by research project and can be shared with collaborators.

Share your research questions, how Kimi could help, and how you'll validate the results.

items.title: @ylecun
items.summary:
JEPA has been something we follow very closely, and over the last couple of weeks, @ylecun and his collaborators at AMI Labs, NYU, and Brown have made huge progress with it.

I reached out to @randall_balestr , who co-authored "Counterfactual World Models", to ask what he found most interesting in the paper. He told me that touch might be the frontier of what offline data can teach a robot. A video of a hand barely missing a mug doesn't tell you what would've happened if it had touched it. Maybe robots need to try things for themselves to learn.

That conversation inspired me to make this video. I walk through two papers in detail (but keep it accessible):

1. The Content–Geometry Tradeoff in World Models:

A JEPA can learn the layout of a city walk from first-person views and movement commands, without GPS! But in a separate experiment, it can lose track of a cube sitting right in front of it. The proposed fix, Slow SVReg, helps the model hold on to details that don’t change much from one frame to the next.

2. JEPAs that ask “What if?” (Counterfactual World Models)

Say a current pushed your boat off course. Where would you have ended up if you’d steered left in that same current? With residual reuse, you take the gap between where you landed and where JEPA predicted you’d land, then add it to the prediction for steering left.

Watch this video explainer to see the whole picture with demos, visuals, and Randall's full note to get a feel for it.

Also, on Youtube youtube.com/watch?v=oaIgPi4O…
